Edge of the Woods
At first the woods are just a few trees spread out through the fields, as 
though there were territorial creatures each wanting their own piece of ground. 
A few steps more and the trees begin to crowd in. A few steps beyond that and 
the branches intertwine overhead so that the sunlight becomes filtered and 
scattered by the dense canopy of leaves.

You follow a bend in the trail. The air becomes cooler, the light more shadowed.

...and a wolf steps slowly onto the path in front of you.

You freeze in your tracks and a few seconds pass while you stare into his shiny 
red eyes.

He speaks. His voice is low and gravelly, every word is just shy of a growl: 
"Good day, little girl."

. . .

events.intent: Go southwest toward woods
Describe Edge of Woods during wolf encounter
events.response:
Never stray from the path. Never talk to strangers.

Your mother's prohibitions rush into your mind, knocking all other thoughts to 
the side. Anger follows, anger at your mother for treating you like a child. 
Anger, you're a bit surprised to notice, but not fear. You're not afraid of the 
wolf at all...

. . .

events.intent: Press Return to continue wolf conversation pause
events.response:
He smiles. "Where are you headed so early, in that pretty red cape?"

You smile too and suddenly you're feeling shy. When you respond, you look down 
at your hands both clutching the handle of the basket. "To my grandmother's 
house in the woods."

"And what have you got there in your basket?" Although you don't look up, you 
can hear that he's still smiling.

Growing in confidence, you look up, meeting his eyes again: "I have bread and 
honey, and a bottle of wine. Yesterday was baking day, so I'm taking some 
things to help my poor, sick grandmother get stronger."

He considers your statement with a slow nod. He looks, what? Impressed? Or at 
least appreciative of your good deed...

. . .

events.intent: Press Return to continue wolf dialogue
events.response:
"Where does your grandmother live, little red-cape?"

"A good ways farther into the woods. Her house stands under three big oak 
trees, and on the slope below are a stand of beech trees." Then, feeling 
playful, you add, "Surely if you live in the forest you must already know for 
yourself where her house is."

But this little taunt seems to miss the mark. He doesn't respond. His nose is 
up, but his eyes are down. After several moments, he raises one eyebrow. He 
blinks slowly. His eyes meet yours. "May I walk with you for a bit?"

You nod. The two of you walk together in silence, while your mind and heart 
race with new feelings. You lose track of time.

. . .

events.intent: Press Return to continue wolf walk

"All this time you've been walking along with such concentration, as though you 
were on your way to school. But it's so cheery out here! See how beautiful the 
flowers are! You'd have walked right past them."

For the first time you notice that you're standing in a field of wildflowers. 
The lush green grass is everywhere splattered with droplets of yellow, purple, 
white... You imagine the first drops of rain falling on the steps of your front 
porch, how the droplets make dark wet flowers on the dry wood. The flowers and 
the grass of the glen all sway in a breeze so gentle you can barely feel it 
against your skin.

You turn, beaming, eager to share this moment with the wolf...

But when you look to your side, he is gone.

throat. The wolf, however, is in a more powerful position and quickly overcomes 
him. Through the cracks in the floor of the attic crawlspace, you watch your 
father die.

tear-filled eyes record every detail of the scene, charring the images into

its back. Though it may never keep time again, you can read the upturned face

events.intent: Go west to wooded path
events.response:
Wooded Path
Several trails converge here, and you recall how relieved you were that 
grandmother met you at the bridge the first few times you made the trip from 
home without mother. Now, you are certain of the right way: the northwest path 
leads to grandmother's house and the southern path leads back across the 
covered bridge. Other paths lead east and northeast.

The trail of shining stones enters this clearing along the path from the 
northwest, but then turns abruptly, abandoning the well-marked path and leading 
east into the forest.

You have a sense that the locket around your neck recognizes your surroundings. 
Charged by the moonlight, the locket becomes hot and your vision becomes dark. 
Your body fades and other sensations come into focus.

"This way, children." The large man, your father, points his axe east and steps 
off the path into the underbrush.

You don't follow. But you watch two other figures -- a boy and a woman -- 
follow obediently.

You've learned from your experiences with grandmother's locket that you're not 
looking through your own eyes, but through hers. The bodily sensations feel 
like your own, though, and there's no mistaking the sensations you feel when 
you see the woman. Your lip curls, your eyes squint, your eyebrows furrow. The 
muscles in your shoulders and arms flex. Your hands curl into fists.

Rage. You hate this woman. You hate her for who she's trying to be, and you 
hate her for what she's doing to father, and you hate father for letting her do 
it, and you won't follow them into the woods because you know it's her idea.

You are pulled from this whirlpool of thoughts by the boy. He's come back. 
"Sister? It's going to be all right, remember?" He speaks calmly and quietly. 
He thinks you're scared... and you are a little, although your fear is nothing 
compared to your fury.

His tone relaxes you more than his words. "Remember? I've got a plan for this."

The locket cools. The vision subsides. You regain your own senses.

The thick glass of the lens tells you that whoever wore it must have had 
terrible eyesight. Who could it have belonged to? You know that grandmother's 
vision was fine... but her father, her brother, her husband? Perhaps it 
belonged to one of them...

As you turn your attention to the monocle, grandmother's locket again grows hot 
against the skin of your throat. Again, the heat cascades out, washing away 
your body, flooding your mind with foreign memories...

You crouch, huddled tightly against the side of the unusual, unfamiliar house. 
When she appears, you see her first from the back. She steps out onto the 
stoop, scanning the woods in front of the house. She's looking for you.

Despite her long black hair -- brilliant in the scattered sunlight of the 
woods, spilling over her shoulders from beneath an orange headscarf -- she 
reaches for the railing with an ancient hand, a bony snarl of knuckles under 
loose olive-colored skin.

She's muttering something as she slowly descends the few stairs to the ground. 
The syllables are fast, the words are foreign. Then, still peering away into 
the woods, she calls out. This time you understand the words, but only with 
difficulty. She speaks your language with a honey-thick accent.

"The wind, eh? I heard you nibbling... Where are you, my little children of the 
sky?"

She reaches into the pocket of her apron, withdraws the thick monocle, and 
raises it to her right eye. Her head scans left and right, and she takes a few 
quick steps, zigzagging and lifting her legs high as though to avoid invisible 
obstacles. Suddenly, she freezes. Fear traps your heart.

She turns so slowly that you begin to sweat in suspense and anticipation. 
You're caught by her ember-red eyes -- one dim, one bright and magnified by the 
monocle -- and the world goes black around you.

The locket cools. The vision subsides. You regain your own senses.

Burned Ground
This patch of the woods is dead: black and burnt with no living plant rooting 
in the soil. Life crawls up to the edge of the dead patch but stops abruptly. 
The long blades of grass don't even hang over the perimeter. Larger plants -- 
the bramble thicket, a large oak tree -- live somewhat farther back. The leaves 
of the oak hang over this clearing making it even darker than the rest of the 
forest.

Perhaps there was a fire? But when? Grandmother never said anything about a 
fire. And how long would it take for the forest to reclaim a burned patch of 
ground? Whatever is was, you have a decidedly uneasy feeling about this place.

You have a sense that the locket around your neck recognizes your surroundings. 
Your body fades and other sensations come into focus.

The first day all you felt was anger: anger at your stepmother for dreaming up 
such a heartless idea, anger at your father for going along with it (twice!), 
anger at your brother for his inept plan. This last feeling was the hardest to 
admit. The first time, his plan had worked flawlessly. And yes, when the two of 
you had heard that your parents -- correction: your father and stepmother -- 
were going to try again to abandon you in the forest, he had tried to prepare. 
But breadcrumbs? How could he have ever thought that would work?

By the second day, the anger was supplanted by fear. How were you going to find 
your way home? What were you going to eat? Were you going to die out here?

This morning you awoke to face your third day in the woods and every feeling, 
every thought had been replaced by the sour ache of hunger in your stomach.

Hoping that the animals of the forest know where to find food, you have tracked 
a white bird to this spot. You watch the bird settle into its nest among the 
branches of the large oak tree and you stop to take in your surroundings... and 
you see the little house. Instantly, your starving brain becomes delirious with 
the possibility of rescue and you run for the front steps.

When your brother grabs your arm, you spin around ready to scream at him for 
slowing you down. But the look on his face makes you stop. He's staring over 
your shoulder at the house. His jaw is slack and he's starting to drool. 
Without looking at you, he asks a question that would never have even crossed 
your mind...

"Gretel, what is that house made of?"

The locket cools. The vision subsides. You regain your own senses.
